blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The  2025  Medium-Term  Debt  Management  Strategy  (MTDS)  has  been  prepared  in accordance with Section 33 (2) of the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012. It serves as a roadmap for the management of the country's public debt for the period FY 2025/26-2027/28. It outlines the strategies and initiatives aimed at minimizing costs and management of risks of debt over the medium term.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Public and publicly guaranteed debt stock increased to Ksh. 10,581.98 billion as of the end of June 2024 from Ksh. 10,278.88 billion as of the end of June 2023. This comprises an external debt stock of Ksh. 5,171.70 billion and a domestic debt stock of Ksh. 5,410.28 billion.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The October 2024 Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) reports Kenya's public debt to be sustainable but with a high risk of debt distress. The present value (PV) of public debt was 63.0 percent of GDP against the benchmark debt threshold of 55 percent of debt to GDP. The National Treasury has until 1 st   November 2028 to bring the present value of public debt to within the threshold.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The MTDS has been prepared in an environment of vibrant economic growth but a volatile financial market globally and locally. The domestic economy grew by 5.0 percent in the first quarter and 4.6 percent in the second quarter of 2024. Kenya's economic performance is projected to remain stable over the medium term. Growth is expected to moderate to 5.2 percent in 2024 and 5.4 percent in 2025 from 5.6 percent in 2023. Growth will be largely driven by broad-based private sector activities and ongoing government interventions and strategies under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The 2025 debt management strategy seeks to gradually reduce the stock of Treasury bills while lengthening maturity of public debt instruments and deepening the domestic debt market  through  issuance  of  medium  to  long  term  debt  securities  accompanied  by  debt market reforms. From the external sources, the strategy proposes a mix of concessional and commercial borrowing.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The strategy aims at 25 percent and 75 percent gross borrowing from external and domestic sources, respectively.Net borrowing to finance fiscal deficits is structured into 65 percent and 35 percent from domestic and external sources, respectively.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: I. INTRODUCTION
heading_path: I. INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy (MTDS) is the policy framework that guides government borrowing and public debt management. The framework guides the Government in pursuing a desired structure of the public debt portfolio which reflects costs and risks trade-offs, to support the fiscal deficit path outlined in the Budget Policy Statement (BPS).
heading_path: I. INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The  preparation  and  submission  of  the  2025  MTDS  for  the  period  FY  2025/26  to 2027/28 is in accordance with sections 33(2) and 63(c) of Public Finance Management Act, 2012.
heading_path: I. INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The National Treasury is mandated to manage the levels and composition of public debt, including guarantees and other financial obligations as provided for in sections 12 (1) (b) and 62(b) of the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012.
heading_path: I. INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The 2025 debt management strategy aims at:
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Reducing refinancing risks by reducing short maturities debt while lengthening  the  total  portfolio  Average  Time  to  Maturity  (ATM)  by deepening the domestic bond market through issuance of more medium to long term instruments as the main source of domestic financing;
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Reducing the interest rate risk by increasing the Average Time to Refixing and reducing the amount of debt with variable interest rates;
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Reducing  the  foreign  exchange  risk  by  diversifying  debt  held  in  foreign currencies; and
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Promoting intergenerational equity.
heading_path: a) Objectives of the 2025 Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: b) Scope of the MTDS
heading_path: b) Scope of the MTDS

blocks.text: The MTDS analysis takes into account outstanding public debt and projected borrowing and debt service in the context of ongoing and projected macroeconomic environment and  the  conditions  in  the  international  and  domestic  capital  markets.  Performing guaranteed debt and other local debts and overdraft are excluded from the proposed debt management strategies.  Debts excluded amounts to Ksh. 263.74 billion which includes Ksh.100.17 billion uncalled guaranteed debts, Ksh. 61.03 billion Government overdraft at CBK, Ksh.13.54 billion Suppliers credit, Ksh. 83.54 IMF SDR Allocation and Ksh. 5.47 billion Bank advances.
heading_path: b) Scope of the MTDS

blocks.text: c) Organisation of the document
heading_path: c) Organisation of the document

blocks.text: The succeeding sections comprise of: Review of the Existing Public Debt Portfolio; Analysis of Costs and Risks of Existing Public Debt; Review of Performance of the 2023 MTDS;  Kenya's  Debt Sustainability; Challenges to Debt Management; Macroeconomic Assumptions and Key Risks; Potential Sources of Financing; Debt Management Strategy; Strategy Implementation, Monitoring, Evaluation; and Annexes.

heading_path: II. REVIEW OF THE EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT STOCK

blocks.text: As at end June 2024, the stock of public debt was Ksh. 10,581.98 billion (65.7 percent of GDP), equivalent to USD 81.70 billion in nominal terms, of which domestic debt was Ksh. 5,410.28 billion while external debt was Ksh. 5,171.70 billion ( Table 1 ).
heading_path: II. REVIEW OF THE EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT STOCK

blocks.text: The 2025 MTDS analysis takes into account debt stock of Ksh. 10,318.25 billion or USD 79.66 billion excluding the performing guarantees debts, IMF SDR Allocation, Government overdraft at Central Bank of Kenya (CBK), Suppliers credit and Bank advances.

blocks.text: III. ANALYSIS OF COSTS AND RISKS OF EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT
heading_path: III. ANALYSIS OF COSTS AND RISKS OF EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT

blocks.text: This section highlights the costs and risks characteristics of the existing public debt portfolio as at end June 2024.
heading_path: III. ANALYSIS OF COSTS AND RISKS OF EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT

blocks.text: Nominal debt as a percentage of GDP declined to 65.7 percent in June 2024 from 72.0 percent in June 2023 due to appreciation of Kenya shilling against major currencies while  the  present  value  of  public  debt  to  GDP  declined  to  63.0  percent  from  68.2 percent in the same period ( Table 3 ).
heading_path: III. ANALYSIS OF COSTS AND RISKS OF EXISTING PUBLIC DEBT

blocks.text: The domestic debt with maturity of 4 to 10 years improved as at end June 2024. The proportion of instruments with less than one year to maturity increased to 18.6 percent as at end June 2024 from 16.7 percent as at end June 2023 and this was attributed to the National Treasury uptake of short-term instruments. As a result, the proportion of instruments with maturity of 2-3 years and greater than 11 years as at end June 2024 reduced from 15.3 percent and 26.9 percent as at end June 2023 to 13.5 percent and 22.2 percent as at end June 2024, respectively ( Table 4 ).

blocks.text: IV. REVIEW OF PERFOMANCE OF THE 2023 MTDS
heading_path: IV. REVIEW OF PERFOMANCE OF THE 2023 MTDS

blocks.text: The FY 2023/24 MTDS aimed at maximizing use of concessional funding and rollover of  commercial  debt  from  external  borrowing  accompanied by liability management operations whereas on the domestic borrowing front, the target was to lengthen the maturity profile and mitigate refinancing risk through issuance of medium to long term benchmark Treasury bonds.
heading_path: IV. REVIEW OF PERFOMANCE OF THE 2023 MTDS

blocks.text: Whereas the overall strategy was to minimize costs and risks through a net financing mix of 50 per cent from both external and domestic sources, the outcome was in the ratio 73:27 net domestic to external financing, as reported in Budget Outturn (2024 Budget review and outlook paper) ( Table 5 ).
heading_path: IV. REVIEW OF PERFOMANCE OF THE 2023 MTDS

blocks.text: The deviation was attributed to limited access to external financing which resulted to more  uptake  of  borrowing  from  domestic  sources.  In  FY  2023/2024,  Kenya's  net domestic financing was Ksh. 595.57 billion, or 89 per cent of the target.  From external financing, the net amount was Ksh. 222.75 billion, or 86 per cent of the target during the fiscal year.
heading_path: IV. REVIEW OF PERFOMANCE OF THE 2023 MTDS

blocks.text: In  February  2024,  The  National  Treasury  successfully  refinanced  USD 1.50 billion (75%) of the USD 2.00 billion Eurobond maturity through issuance of international Eurobond, with the remaining USD 500 million repaid from the exchequer in June 2024. The actual gross external borrowing in the period was 25.0 percent of the total public borrowing, which was below 35.0 percent target ( Table 6 ).

blocks.text: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: The public debt 1 remains sustainable but with high risk of debt distress.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: External Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) demonstrates that the Present Value (PV) of  the  external  debt  to  GDP  ratio  is  below  the  40  percent  sustainability  threshold throughout the projection period. The PV of Public and Publicly Guaranteed (PPG) external  debt-to-exports  remains  above  the  sustainability  threshold  of  180  percent through 2029.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: The debt service to revenue ratio breaches the threshold of 18 percent from 2024 to 2028 due to heavy maturities during the period. Debt service-to-exports remains above the sustainability threshold of 15 percent through to 2029 ( Table 8 ).
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: The Present Value (PV) of total public debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to remain above the 55 percent benchmark through 2029 ( Table 9 ), after which it is projected to decline to within the approved threshold.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: Policy initiatives by the Government are necessary to diversify and/or expand export base and build gross international reserves to improve the external debt sustainability ratios.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: The  Government  will  sustain  fiscal  consolidation  efforts  over  the  medium  term  to create fiscal space and reduce debt related risks. The Government will also continue to optimize the use of external concessional funding and lengthen the maturity profile of public debt through issuance of medium to long dated bonds.

blocks.text: The Government will explore possibilities of various Liability Management Operations (LMOs) options with the aim of extending the maturity of existing debt to reduce near term maturities. In addition, a steady and strong outlook for exports will play a major role in supporting external debt sustainability.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: For  public  debt  to  continue  on  a  sustainable  path,  there  is  need  to  reduce  annual borrowing limits (fiscal deficits) to slow the rate of debt accumulation.
heading_path: V. KENYA'S DEBT SUSTAINABILITY

blocks.text: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Kenya's recent downgrade in credit rating has a significant impact on the financial terms of various credit sources especially the commercial. Rating downgrades may lead to increased borrowing costs, limited access to credit markets, low investor confidence, currency depreciation, and debt sustainability risk.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Public debt legal framework not empowering enough as does not provide the PDMO with requisite autonomy to manage public debt.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Duplicated legal provisions-CBK Act, PFM Act 2012 providing CBK with leverage unqualified fiscal agency privileges without adequate accountability.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Tight  budget  provisions  precipitate  cash  constraints  leading  to  borrowing  proceeds being a major budget funding source.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Deteriorating sovereign credit ratings due to debt accumulation on account of fiscal deficits.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Large share of foreign currency debt leading to exchange rate risks.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Changing  Regulatory  Environment:  adapting  to  evolving  lending  patterns  and ensuring adherence to international standards is very demanding.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: External Market Volatility: External factors such as global market volatility, interest rate fluctuations, and low credit ratings impact debt management strategies.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Legal reforms required to deepen domestic market are slow and difficult to come due to duplicated authority among the fiscal agent and National Treasury.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Limited understanding in public debt management amongst major stakeholders.  Public debt is both a highly technical and an emotive subject in the political arena. Need for a sustained capacity building on public debt management (it affects citizen welfare).
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: High stock of maturing Treasury bills exert pressure on liquidity and hence the need to reduce Treasury bills  Stock. There is need to reduce refinancing risk by  separating borrowing  operations  of  the  PDMO  from  liquidity  management  operations  of  the Exchequer.
heading_path: VI. CHALLENGES TO DEBT MANAGEMENT

blocks.text: Underperformance  of  Government  Securities  auctions  may  affect  borrowing performance.
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: Failure  to  absorb  external  financing  from  creditors  may  lead  to  reduced underfunding of the budget.
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: Underperformance  in revenue collection leading to increased debt accumulation.
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: The risk of depreciation of Kenya shilling against major currencies may increase fiscal pressure and pass-through inflation.
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: Materialization of fiscal risks and contingent liabilities arising from state-owned enterprises debt defaults.
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: Risk of further credit downgrade
heading_path: b) Key Risks to Macroeconomic Assumptions

blocks.text: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: The  domestic  and  external  markets  are  the  main  sources  of  Government  deficit financing.
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: The  government  will  raise  funds  from  the  domestic  market  through  issuance  of Treasury bonds and bills.
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: The National Treasury will spearhead key reforms that deepen the market and diversify the investor base. To enhance the growth of the non-bank financial institutions such as pension, insurance and mutual funds, there is need to expand the volumes and initiate new  financial  products  such  as  post-retirement  and  contributory  pension  schemes, diversified asset classes, private equity and venture capital.
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: The external borrowing will be through concessional loans from multilateral, bilateral and limited commercial loans such as international bond issuances.
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: The Government will also explore emerging funding instruments such as debt swaps, diaspora bond, sustainability linked bonds and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) debt instruments to fund budget deficit and manage public debt.
heading_path: VIII. POTENTIAL SOURCES OF FINANCING

blocks.text: IX. DEBT MANAGEMENT STRATEGY
heading_path: IX. DEBT MANAGEMENT STRATEGY

blocks.text: a) Analysis of Costs and  Risks Indicators Under  Alternative  Debt Management Strategies
heading_path: a) Analysis of Costs and  Risks Indicators Under  Alternative  Debt Management Strategies

blocks.text: Analysis of various borrowing mixes and strategies has been undertaken to identify the mix and the strategy that minimises public debt costs and reduces risks to overall public debt.
heading_path: a) Analysis of Costs and  Risks Indicators Under  Alternative  Debt Management Strategies

blocks.text: Table  11  shows  the  costs  and  risks  indicators  of  the  four  alternative  strategies  and Annexes 1 to 4 shows more details of the alternative debt management strategies. From array of strategies below analysed in Table 11 below Strategy 2 (S2) provides more prospective benefits in terms of costs and risks of public debt than any other alternative strategy.
heading_path: a) Analysis of Costs and  Risks Indicators Under  Alternative  Debt Management Strategies

blocks.text: Table 11: Expected Costs and Risks Indicators Under Alternative Strategies
heading_path: a) Analysis of Costs and  Risks Indicators Under  Alternative  Debt Management Strategies

blocks.text: b) 2025 Overall Debt Management Strategy
heading_path: b) 2025 Overall Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The gross borrowing is 25 percent external and 75 percent domestic. From the domestic sources, the target is to gradually reduce the stock of Treasury bills while lengthening debt maturity and issuance of medium to long term debt securities. On the external end, the target is to have a mix of concessional and commercial borrowing. Gross external financing would be composed of 11 percent concessional, 1 percent semi-concessional and 13 percent commercial borrowing. The expected composition of public debt at the end of  the  Strategy  period  will  be  46  percent  external  and  54  percent  domestic,  as shown in Annex 2.
heading_path: b) 2025 Overall Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: c) Deficit Financing Strategy (FY 2025/26-2027/28)
heading_path: c) Deficit Financing Strategy (FY 2025/26-2027/28)

blocks.text: The MTDS analytical tool has guided that a net borrowing mix of 65 percent and 35 percent from domestic and external sources respectively will help optimize costs and risks of financing the fiscal deficits for the MTDS period 2025-2028.
heading_path: c) Deficit Financing Strategy (FY 2025/26-2027/28)

blocks.text: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: Implementation  of  the  strategy  will  improve  the  debt  sustainability  indicators  by reducing nominal debt to GDP to 52.8 percent from the current 65.7 percent and the present value of debt to GDP from 63.0 percent to 48.6 percent over the implementation period by FY2027/28 ( Table 12 ).
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: The debt burden will significantly reduce as shown in the reduced interest payment as a  percentage  of  GDP  to  4.4  per  cent  from  the  current  5.4  per  cent.  Lower  interest payments imply reduced pressure on the budget, which can free up resources for other priorities.
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: In terms of refinancing risks, the optimal strategy reduces the risk by lowering the debt maturing in 1 year as a percentage of GDP and lengthening the debt maturity both in the domestic and external portfolio.
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: The Strategy reduces the interest rate risk greatly by increasing the Average Time to Refixing to 8.2 years from 7.3 years, increasing the debt with fixed rates from 85.2 per cent to 92.1 per cent, and reducing the amount of Treasury bills in the portfolio to 3.9 per cent from the current 5.1 per cent.
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: In terms of exchange rate risk, it reduces the foreign exchange risk from 49.3 per cent to 45.5 per cent by focusing on borrowing more from the domestic debt market.
heading_path: d) Expected Costs and Risks Indicators in 2028

blocks.text: e) Risks to the Strategy
heading_path: e) Risks to the Strategy

blocks.text: Factors that could lead to the optimal strategy not being fully implemented may include emergency conditions like auction failure, widening of the deficit, limited access to external funding which could disrupt financing plan, and default on guarantees.

blocks.text: X. STRATEGY IMPLEMENTATION, MONITORING AND EVALUATION
heading_path: X. STRATEGY IMPLEMENTATION, MONITORING AND EVALUATION

blocks.text: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: 76. The Government will implement the debt management strategy through the Annual Borrowing Plan (ABP). The implementation work plan is shown in Table 13 below.
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: Table 13: MTDS Implementation Work Plan
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: PDMO will prepare domestic and external borrowing plan comprising of projected borrowing and settlement of maturities within the 2025/26 fiscal year.
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: The external borrowing plan will comprise of expected disbursements by each creditor, the disbursement period and currency of disbursement within the fiscal year as per the 2025 MTDS.
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: The ABP may be revised to include liability management operations to manage debt stock risks when market conditions allow.
heading_path: a) Domestic and External Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: b) Review of the Borrowing Plan
heading_path: b) Review of the Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: Review  of  the  outcome  of  implementation  of  the  Borrowing  Plan  will  be  done  on weekly, monthly and on annual basis to provide data for strategy evaluation and for public information.
heading_path: b) Review of the Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: The progress of implementation of the 2025 MTDS will be monitored and reported through monthly reports and the Annual Public Debt Management Report (APDMR) which is prepared and published after the end of the fiscal year.
heading_path: b) Review of the Borrowing Plan

blocks.text: c) Monitoring and Review of Cost and Risk Indicator Outturn of the Strategy
heading_path: c) Monitoring and Review of Cost and Risk Indicator Outturn of the Strategy

blocks.text: The costs and risks outcome characteristics in the 2025 MTDS will be evaluated semiannually and annually against sustainability threshold indicators to determine deviations  and  suggest  mitigation  measures.  Table  13  outlines  the  costs  and  risks parameters to be evaluated.
heading_path: c) Monitoring and Review of Cost and Risk Indicator Outturn of the Strategy

blocks.text: The evolving public debt structure and fiscal deficit will inform review of strategy for management of costs and risks of public debt going forward. In addition, any deviations will be used to inform strategy review and formulation of the MTDS in the next cycle.
heading_path: c) Monitoring and Review of Cost and Risk Indicator Outturn of the Strategy

blocks.text: Similarly, guaranteed State-Owned  Enterprises' debt, fiscal  commitments  and contingent  liabilities will  be tracked  and  assessed  against  overall  public  debt sustainability levels.

blocks.text: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The pricing assumptions under the baseline scenario for interest rates and the exchange rates are as follows:
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: ADF loans are priced at an average fixed rate of 0.75 percent, with a 40-year tenor and upto 10-year grace period.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: IDA/IFAD loans are priced at an average fixed rate of 2.0 percent, with a 30-year tenor and up-to 10-year grace period.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Other concessional loans are priced at an average fixed rate of 2.0 percent, with a 28-year tenor and up-to 7-year grace period.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Semi-concessional  loans  are  assumed  to  be  contracted  at  a  fixed  interest  rate  of approximately 3.0 percent and a maturity of 23 years including a grace period of up to 5 years.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Commercial  borrowings  and  Export  Credit  Agencies  financing  with  floating  rates  are contracted at a reference rate plus a margin.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The pricing of Kenya's International Sovereign debt is based on US forward rates and credit spread.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Pricing on the domestic debt instruments is based on US forward rates, credit spread and inflation differential.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The  outlook  on  the  baseline  interest  rates  and  exchange  rates  is  based  on  the  following considerations;
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The  exchange  rate  (Ksh/USD)  is  assumed  to  depreciate  annually  at  an  average  of 2.8 percent.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The fixed interest rates  of market-based instruments in the international capital markets were based on US forward rates and credit spread. The domestic market yields were based on US forward rates, credit spread and inflation differential.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The  interest  rates  for  fixed  rate  loans  are  assumed  to  remain  priced  as  per  the  existing portfolio.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Three risk scenarios are evaluated as follows:
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The risk scenario for interest rates assumes moderate interest rate shock of 0.75 percent and 1.5 percent in 2026 and 2027 respectively and a stand-alone extreme shock of 1.5 percent and 3.0 percent over the same period.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The risk scenario for exchange rate assumes a stand-alone extreme shock of 25 percent in 2026 which was applied on the baseline exchange rate projections.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: The combined exchange rate and interest rate risk shock scenario assumes an increase in interest rate by a moderate shock of 0.75 percent combined with a 12.5 percent exchange rate depreciation in 2026.
heading_path: Annex 5: Baseline Pricing Assumptions and Description of Shock Scenarios

blocks.text: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Section 33 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 provides:
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: On or before 15th February in each year, the Cabinet Secretary shall submit to Parliament a statement setting out the debt management strategy of the national government over the medium term with respect to its actual liability in respect of loans and guarantees and its plans for dealing with those liabilities.
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The  Cabinet  Secretary  shall  ensure  that  the  medium-term  debt  management strategy is aligned to the broad strategic priorities and policy goals set out in the Budget Policy Statement.
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The Cabinet Secretary shall include in the statement the following information: -
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The total stock of debt as at the date of the statement;
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The sources of loans made to the national government and the nature of guarantees given by the national government;
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The principal risks associated with those loans and guarantees;
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: The assumptions underlying the debt management strategy; and
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: An analysis of the sustainability of the amount of debt, both actual and potential.
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: Within fourteen days  after  the  debt  strategy  paper  is  submitted  to  Parliament under  this  section,  the  Cabinet  Secretary  shall  submit  the  statement  to  the Commission  on  Revenue  Allocation  and  the  Intergovernmental  Budget  and Economic Council, publish, and publicize the statement.
heading_path: Annex 6: Publication of the Debt Management Strategy

blocks.text: PFM Act 2012, 'General responsibilities of the National Treasury' Section 12. Provides that: (1) Subject to the Constitution and this Act, the National Treasury shall- (b) manage the level and composition of national public debt, national guarantees  and  other  financial  obligations  of  national  government  within  the framework of this Act and develop a framework for sustainable debt control.
